extracted.subtask_description: A newsroom style and usage guide of terms related to race, religion, disability, gender, nationality and other identity topics, with guidance on preferred wording, capitalization, when to disclose diagnoses/identities and cautions about stereotypes and offensive terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allahu akbar
rubrics_metrics.description: In Arabic it means “God is great” or “God is the greatest.” Muslims say it several times a day, such as during the call for prayer, during prayer, when they are happy and when they wish to express their approval of what they hear.

rubrics_metrics.name: ally
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who makes the commitment and effort to recognize their privilege (based on gender, class, race, sexual identity, etc.) and work in solidarity with oppressed groups in the struggle for justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allies understand it is in their interest to end forms of oppression, commit to reducing their own complicity, and invest in strengthening their own knowledge and awareness of oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alzheimer's disease
rubrics_metrics.description: A progressive and fatal disease in which nerve cells in the brain degenerate and brain matter shrinks, resulting in impaired thinking, behavior and memory. The Alzheimer’s Association identifies it as the most common form of dementia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the proper term Alzheimer’s disease (never Alzheimer’s). Disclose that an individual has Alzheimer’s disease only if relevant to the story and the person has been formally diagnosed by a licensed medical professional. Refer to the subject as someone who has Alzheimer’s disease rather than using 'suffers from' or 'afflicted with.'

rubrics_metrics.name: America
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to the entire Western hemisphere and does not apply solely to the United States. North America and South America together are often referred to as the Americas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When referring to the United States of America, use United States, U.S., U.S.A. or the States.

rubrics_metrics.name: American
rubrics_metrics.description: People who live in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that many people in other parts of the Americas see themselves as Americans; some view the national identity label as imperialist. 'American' is the most widely recognized term for people who live in the United States of America.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Indian
rubrics_metrics.description: American Indian and Native American are both generally acceptable and can be used interchangeably, although individuals may have a preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Native American and American Indian interchangeably for groups; journalists should always identify people by their preferred tribal affiliation when reporting on individuals. Use native-born to describe someone born in the United States but not American Indian. Note federal recognition and that tribes determine their own membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Indian Movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Activist organization known as AIM. Founded in 1968 to promote civil rights for Native Americans and to seek recognition of treaty rights through protests.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Indian or Alaska Native, U.S. Census definition of
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Census Bureau defines American Indian or Alaska Native as 'a person having origins in any of the original peoples of North and South America (including Central America) and who maintains tribal affiliation or community attachment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The racial categories reflect social definitions of race, not biological definitions; categories may include racial and national origin or sociocultural groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Sign Language
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete language that utilizes signs made by moving the hands combined with facial expressions and postures of the body; used by many deaf or hard of hearing people in North America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify American Sign Language on first reference, capitalizing all three words. ASL is acceptable on second reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal civil rights legislation created in 1990 to address discrimination on the basis of disability in employment, public accommodations, transportation and telecommunications as well as state and local government services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Americans with Disabilities Act on first reference; ADA is acceptable on second reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amish
rubrics_metrics.description: Descendants of the Swiss Anabaptists, known for plain clothes and in some cases rejection of modern technology; base morals on the Bible and unwritten rules called the Ordnung.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amish pastors are called bishops.

rubrics_metrics.name: amputation, amputee
rubrics_metrics.description: Amputation refers to removal of a bodily extremity, usually during surgery. Amputee is the acceptable term for someone who has undergone an amputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Someone with an amputation or amputee are both acceptable; distinguish from congenital physical deformity that is not a result of amputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: anchor baby, anchor child
rubrics_metrics.description: A child born to a non-citizen mother in a country that grants automatic citizenship to children born on its soil; the term is pejorative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the term except in quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: androgyne
rubrics_metrics.description: A person whose biological sex is not readily apparent or who is between two genders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best to ask people who identify as androgyne which pronouns they prefer; see related entries agender, genderqueer, non-binary gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: androphilic, gynephilic
rubrics_metrics.description: Attraction to males/masculinity (andro) or females/femininity (gyne).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms are alternatives to homosexual or heterosexual to avoid gendering the person while expressing attraction to a particular gender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angel Island
rubrics_metrics.description: The West Coast counterpart to Ellis Island; U.S. Immigration Station processed many immigrants (majority from China) from 1910 to 1940 and later housed POWs in WWII.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Angel Island is now a state park; virtual tour available from Angel Island Immigration Station Foundation.

rubrics_metrics.name: annul, annulment
rubrics_metrics.description: In Catholic Church context, an annulment (declaration of nullity) means the sacramental bond of matrimony never existed because a party was unwilling or unable to make and keep marital promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An annulment does not mean a loving marriage relationship never existed and does not make children illegitimate in church or civil law.

rubrics_metrics.name: antisemitism
rubrics_metrics.description: A prejudice against people of Jewish heritage that has inspired the Holocaust and other crimes. Religious antisemitism is based on the idea that all Jews are collectively responsible for killing Jesus; economic/political antisemitism involves conspiratorial claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is debate about spelling; many organizations favor the unhyphenated 'antisemitism.' Note updated guidance and refer to IHRA, Jewish Virtual Library, ADL for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: apartheid
rubrics_metrics.description: Racial segregation: policy of segregation and political/economic discrimination enforced by white minority government against non-white residents in South Africa from 1948 to 1994.

rubrics_metrics.name: apocalypse, apocalyptic
rubrics_metrics.description: A final cosmic battle between forces of good and evil; for believers it ushers in the reign of God and raises the righteous to everlasting life. The Book of Revelation is the best-known Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowercase 'apocalypse' when referring to the battle ending the world, but uppercase when using the traditional Catholic name for the Book of Revelation. Catholic News Service advises using Revelation instead of Apocalypse except in direct quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arab
rubrics_metrics.description: Refers to a nation or people from an Arabic-speaking country; not synonymous with Muslim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When referring to events in a specific country, name the country rather than generalizing 'Arab.' Do not imply in headlines or text that Arab equals Muslim, holy war or terrorist. Note that Iran is not an Arab country and its people are primarily Persian/Farsi-speaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arab American, American Arab
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. citizen or permanent resident who traces ancestry to, or immigrated from, Arabic-speaking places in the Middle East and North Africa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arab American is preferred over American Arab.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arab League
rubrics_metrics.description: Formally the League of Arab States, an umbrella organization with 22 members across North Africa, Horn of Africa and Southwest Asia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arabian
rubrics_metrics.description: An adjective that refers to Saudi Arabia, the Arabian Peninsula, or things such as an Arabian horse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ethnicity or nationality is relevant, it is more precise to specify the country (Lebanese, Yemeni, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arabic
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of the language spoken in Arab countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally not used as an adjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: argilah, argeelah
rubrics_metrics.description: A water pipe that filters and cools tobacco smoke; usually flavored and known by several names including sheesha and hookah.

rubrics_metrics.name: aromantic
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who does not experience romantic attraction; may or may not be asexual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See asexual.

rubrics_metrics.name: articulate
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling a black person 'articulate' can imply surprise and be insulting, because Standard American English is often seen as 'proper' and associated with white speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid framing 'articulate' as a surprise; be mindful of authenticity issues and implications that speaking well is unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aryan
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally from Sanskrit 'arya' meaning 'noble'; scholarly usage referred to Indo-European language speakers. In the late 19th century the term was adopted into anti-Semitic ideology and Nazism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern usage by white supremacists denotes a non-Jewish white person; be aware of historical and ideological connotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: asexual
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who does not experience sexual attraction. Asexual people may experience other kinds of attraction and can describe romantic attraction along hetero/homo/bi/pan lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ash Wednesday
rubrics_metrics.description: The seventh Wednesday before Easter marking the start of Lent in Western Christianity; practice includes putting ashes on foreheads as a reminder of mortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice common among Roman Catholics, Anglicans, Episcopalians, many Lutherans and increasingly other Protestant churches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ashkenazi
rubrics_metrics.description: A Jew of German, Polish, Austrian or Eastern European descent; historically spoke Yiddish and formed a majority of U.S. Jews until the Holocaust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronounced 'osh-ken-AH-zee.' See Sephardi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asia
rubrics_metrics.description: About 60 percent of the world’s population lives in Asia. Traditionally East Asia, South Asia and Southeast Asia are defined with example countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In American usage 'Asian' often refers to the entire continent but commonly shorthand for East Asians; British usage often refers to South Asians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asia, Central
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution: vague term. Modern definition might include Mongolia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan; historical definitions varied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asia, use and abuse of images from
rubrics_metrics.description: The AAJA Handbook warns that emblematic images (Taj Mahal, Ganges, Great Wall, pagodas, conical hats, rice paddies, etc.) can be appropriate in context but problematic when altered or stereotyped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stereotypical depictions; altering images (e.g., dressing white figures in stereotypical Asian garb) can reinforce racial stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian
rubrics_metrics.description: Caution: a term as broad as European. In some British usage it refers to South Asians; in the U.S. it generally covers the whole continent but often shorthand for East Asians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific (East Asian, South Asian) when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian American
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper term for people who come from Asia or descend from people who lived in Asia. Do not hyphenate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask people how they identify (Asian American or specific ancestry, e.g., Chinese American). Use umbrella term 'South Asian' for Indians, Pakistanis, Bangladeshis; use 'East Asian' for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, etc. (Updated Feb 2021).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian Exclusion Acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws in which Congress barred or sharply restricted immigration of Asians to the United States (e.g., Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, 1924 Oriental Exclusion Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian names
rubrics_metrics.description: Asian names are more complex than European names; clarify family and surname and rules for second reference with interview subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, ask the subject—especially about second-reference rules (e.g., Mr. Mao vs. Mr. Zedong). Consider including pronunciation explainers in text, broadcast or graphics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian religions
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion is an imprecise term in Asia; practices and beliefs (temples, meditation vs. prayer, Buddha as not a god for many) differ sharply from Judeo-Christian-Islamic traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caution and consult specific entries for Buddhism, Confucianism, Hinduism, Islam, Shintoism, Taoism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asian, U.S. Census definition of
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Census Bureau defines Asian as 'a person having origins in any of the original peoples of the Far East, Southeast Asia, or the Indian subcontinent' with examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander is a separate category for peoples of Hawaii, Guam, Samoa and other Pacific Islands. Census categories reflect social definitions, not biological ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asiatic
rubrics_metrics.description: A 19th-century adjective used in European colonial contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid; it is a vestige of colonialism and imperialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: ASL
rubrics_metrics.description: See American Sign Language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asperger's syndrome
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a distinct diagnosis, now part of autism spectrum disorder; common behaviors include difficulties in social interaction and obsession with specific topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having Asperger’s syndrome only if relevant and formally diagnosed by a licensed medical professional. If specifically diagnosed, refer to a person diagnosed with Asperger’s syndrome or a person with Asperger’s syndrome. Note 'syndrome' not capitalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: assisted living facility
rubrics_metrics.description: A housing option for older people who cannot live independently and need help with medications and daily living activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes referred to as ALFs in the senior living industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: atheist
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who does not believe in God or other supernatural forces. Distinctions exist between 'weak' and 'strong' atheism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See agnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: attention-deficit disorder (ADD)/attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical community now uses ADHD with presentations (predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, combined). Symptoms include restlessness, difficulty focusing and impulsivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having ADD/ADHD only if relevant and formally diagnosed by a licensed medical professional. Use full terms on first reference; ADD/ADHD acceptable on second reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aunt Jemima
rubrics_metrics.description: Nancy Green became the advertising world's first living trademark portraying Aunt Jemima; some view the icon as a painful reminder of slavery and a negative stereotype of black women.

rubrics_metrics.name: aunt, uncle
rubrics_metrics.description: When not referring to a family relationship, the terms may be insensitive or offensive depending on context, historically used by whites for any black person in servitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious; in some communities terms are terms of endearment or respect. In the South, honorifics (Miss, Maam, Aunt, Mister, Uncle, Sir) are traditionally expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: auntie
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cultures a term of respect, not necessarily a family relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an Arab American might call an older Arab female or male 'auntie' ('amty') or 'uncle' ('ammo').

rubrics_metrics.name: autism/autism spectrum disorders
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of complex disorders related to brain development; symptoms vary across the spectrum and include difficulties in communication and restricted/repetitive behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having autism spectrum disorder only if relevant and formally diagnosed. Ask individuals how they prefer to be described; if in doubt, use people-first language (a person with autism spectrum disorder) rather than 'autistic person.'

rubrics_metrics.name: ayatollah
rubrics_metrics.description: A Shiite term for a senior clergyman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize when used as a title before a name, lowercase otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: B.C.
rubrics_metrics.description: Literally before Christ or the Christian era; scholars increasingly use B.C.E. and C.E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See A.D.; consider BCE/CE to avoid Christian-era references.

rubrics_metrics.name: baby boom
rubrics_metrics.description: Any period of greatly increased birth rate; most often refers to post-WWII increase (1946–1964).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: U.S. Census Bureau estimated 76 million Americans born during post-war baby boom; see related Census reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bahá’í, the Bahá’í Faith
rubrics_metrics.description: A monotheistic religion founded by Bahá’u’lláh, teaching progressive revelation and administered by democratically elected councils; no clergy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'the Bahá’í Faith' for the religion and 'Bahá’í' for an adherent. Do not use 'Bahaism' or 'Bahaist.'

rubrics_metrics.name: banana
rubrics_metrics.description: Slang term and pejorative used by Asian Americans for those perceived to identify more with whites than other Asian Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only in direct quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baptist
rubrics_metrics.description: When capitalized, refers to a member of Protestant groups marked by baptism by immersion of individuals who profess faith in Jesus Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry modified to remove the word 'evangelical' from the definition and add 'Protestant.'

rubrics_metrics.name: bar mitzvah, bat mitzvah
rubrics_metrics.description: Milestone in Judaism when a person is responsible for their own actions spiritually and ethically; boys at 13, girls at 12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technically refers to the child becoming bar/bat mitzvah; commonly used to refer to the ceremony. 'Becoming a bar (or bat) mitzvah' is strictly correct, but 'having a bar mitzvah' is common.

rubrics_metrics.name: belonging
rubrics_metrics.description: A sense of fitting in or feeling accepted by a group; feeling valued and respected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently used with diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives and abbreviated DEIB. (Added April 2023)

rubrics_metrics.name: Bible Belt
rubrics_metrics.description: Areas of the U.S. noted for prevalence of strict evangelical Christian teachings, particularly in the South and Midwest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term can be offensive in some contexts; use carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bible-believing
rubrics_metrics.description: A term some Christians use to describe emphasis on authority/primacy of Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using this term except when people use it to describe themselves, since by definition all Christians believe the Bible.

rubrics_metrics.name: bindi, or bindhi
rubrics_metrics.description: Decoration worn on the forehead by many Hindu women with various explanations (symbol of female energy, marriage, third eye, or decoration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronounced 'BIN-dhee.' Worn by Indians of all religions.

rubrics_metrics.name: biological gender/biological sex
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid terms like 'biological gender,' 'biological sex,' 'biological woman/man' as inaccurate and often offensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When necessary refer to assigned sex at birth using terms like 'assigned male at birth' or 'assigned female at birth.' Consider whether the story requires this information; alternatives include 'assigned male/female at birth' or 'raised as a boy/girl.' (Updated March 2021)

rubrics_metrics.name: biphobia
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear of bisexuals often based on stereotypes such as promiscuity or infidelity; intolerance or prejudice is usually a more accurate description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See bisexual.

rubrics_metrics.name: BIPOC
rubrics_metrics.description: Acronym for Black, Indigenous and people of color meant to unite people of color while acknowledging different forms of oppression faced by Black and Indigenous people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BIPOC is a noun; do not say 'BIPOC people' (redundant). Pronounced 'buy-pock.' The term rose to prevalence in 2020; it is commonly used by activists but not universally embraced—some find it redundant. See referenced articles and projects for more discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: bipolar disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental illness characterized by intense shifts in emotion, energy, behavior and activity levels called mood episodes (manic, hypomanic, depressive, mixed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to someone as having bipolar disorder only if the information is central to the story and a licensed medical professional has formally diagnosed the person. Do not use 'bipolar' as an adjective for something that rapidly or drastically changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: biracial, multiracial, mixed-race, two or more races
rubrics_metrics.description: Biracial refers to people of two races; multiracial refers to people of two or more racial backgrounds. Preferred terms include multiracial, biracial, multiethnic, polyethnic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mixed and mixed-race with caution as some find them offensive; others embrace them. (Updated Feb 2021)

rubrics_metrics.name: birth defect
rubrics_metrics.description: See defect/birth defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: bisexual, bi
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who has the capacity to form enduring physical, romantic and/or emotional attractions to those of the same gender or to those of another gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People may experience attraction in differing ways and degrees over their lifetime; prior sexual experiences are not necessary to identify as bisexual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black church
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective noun referring to more than 65,000 Christian churches with a predominance of Black members and clerical leadership; generally refers to Protestants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be more accurate to say 'Black churches' in some contexts. Be mindful many Black people worldwide belong to denominations that are not predominantly Black.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes curtailing rights of African Americans during early Reconstruction (1865-66) aimed to restore political/economic structure of slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also known as Negro Codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Lives Matter, #BlackLivesMatter
rubrics_metrics.description: A civil rights movement started as a Twitter hashtag in 2013 in response to anti-Black racism and police violence; opposes police violence and supports oppressed peoples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written Black Lives Matter or #BlackLivesMatter. According to its website the movement does not believe Black lives are more important than other lives and seeks wide-reaching transformative benefits once Black people are free from oppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Black Muslim
rubrics_metrics.description: Term historically associated with the Nation of Islam and considered derogatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the term. Prefer 'member of the Nation of Islam' and do not use 'Black Muslim' to describe African-American Muslims who practice traditional Islam.
